Battin ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-5361-2033 1 Show authors Nature Water ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research 313 Accesses Metrics details Abstract Glaciers produce abundant grains of reactive minerals that influence inorganic carbon cycling, yet the links between mineral weathering and CO 2 dynamics in glacier-fed streams (GFSs) remain poorly understood. Here we combine streamwater geochemistry, solute end-member modelling, carbonate saturation calculations and suspended-sediment mineralogy across 170 GFSs worldwide. We show that 69% of GFSs were undersaturated with respect to atmospheric CO 2 equilibrium, indicating widespread atmospheric CO 2 uptake. Grain-scale analyses of selected carbonate-bearing GFSs reveal metastable Mg-bearing carbonate phases consistent with secondary mineral formation in transient microenvironments. We propose that CO 2 released during sulfuric acid-driven carbonate weathering and secondary calcite precipitation can be partly consumed by carbonation of silicate- and clay-derived mineral surfaces, transferring dissolved inorganic carbon into particulate inorganic carbon. This sediment-mediated pathway can contribute to CO 2 undersaturation under favourable lithological and geochemical conditions, revealing a previously underappreciated coupling between chemical weathering, sediment–water interactions and inorganic carbon storage in proglacial landscapes rapidly expanding under global glacier retreat. Carbon cycle Hydrology Nutrient and Eutrophication Dynamics in Coastal Ecosystems Main Streams and rivers are major sources of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) to the atmosphere, with global emissions comparable to oceanic sequestration of anthropogenic CO 2 (refs. 1 , 2 ). Groundwater transports CO 2 from terrestrial respiration and chemical rock weathering into streams and rivers, which they vent into the atmosphere through their turbulent surfaces 3 . At the same time, aquatic ecosystem respiration, subsidized by terrestrial organic carbon, further contributes to CO 2 emissions from rivers worldwide. This ecosystem respiration underpins the pronounced heterotrophy of streams and rivers, a concept that has long been central to river carbon cycling research 4 . This biology-centric perspective of the river carbon cycle needs to be better integrated with inorganic carbon cycling, as has been recently emphasized for lakes 5 . The inorganic carbon cycle is particularly important in streams that drain high-latitude and high-altitude catchments above the treeline 6 . These catchments are often within the glacial or periglacial envelope, characterized by high physical erosion, abundant mineral supply and elevated chemical weathering rates. Soils are poorly developed and terrestrial pools of organic carbon are sparse. Glacier-fed streams (GFSs) drain these largely mineral landscapes, which are expanding rapidly due to climate-induced glacier retreat 7 . GFSs themselves are predicted to undergo major changes as glaciers shrink, with some of these alterations affecting their biological carbon cycling. In fact, building evidence suggests that GFSs will become ‘greener’ as increasingly favourable environmental conditions (for example, less turbid waters and reduced discharge) stimulate aquatic primary production 8 . As a consequence, microbial energetics in GFSs may increasingly shift from chemoorganotrophy to heterotrophy 9 . Understanding what this energetic shift may signify for the balance of biological and inorganic carbon cycling in GFSs requires a systematic assessment of inorganic carbon fluxes, including CO 2 exchange with the atmosphere. Today, it remains uncertain whether GFSs globally act as CO 2 sinks or sources to the atmosphere 10 , 11 . An increasing number of local studies provides contrasting insights into CO 2 exchange fluxes in GFSs. Streams draining mafic bedrock in Iceland 12 ; felsic bedrock of the European Alps 13 , Mount Everest 14 and the Qilian Mountains in the northern Tibetan Plateau 15 ; and mixed carbonaceous–felsic lithologies in Alaska 16 and the Canadian Arctic 17 have been reported as net CO 2 sinks.
